Issued at 201 PM CDT Tue Sep 8 2026

The latest RAP analysis and satellite/radar imagery show a 
a cold front extending south across Minnesota early this
afternoon. Ahead of this system, strong southwest flow aloft is 
drawing moisture into the western Great Lakes region, where 
overcast skies and scattered light showers are occurring over
eastern WI. Most of these showers should exit over the next 1-2
hours. While plenty of cloud cover exists over western WI and
Minnesota ahead of the front, portions of the airmass are quite
unstable. Thunderstorms are expected to develop within this
buoyant airmass later this afternoon.

Thunderstorm Potential Tonight...
The primary focus for the short term centers on the aforementioned
cold front, which will sweep across the region tonight. While 
instability will gradually increase from the west through the 
afternoon, the atmosphere will mainly be capped to surface based 
convection despite temperatures rebounding as the rain ends. As a 
result, most guidance is dry after the main area of rain exits 
northeast WI by 2-3 PM. 

Thunderstorm activity will likely develop along the front in a
very buoyant airmass across Minnesota and northern Iowa. This
activity is projected to remain west and south of northeast WI
this evening.

With the approaching front, widely scattered redevelopment of
showers and storms is possible overnight from central to far
northeast WI. Confidence in this redevelopment is relatively low
due to persistent capping and dry air aloft. Patchy ground fog
could develop from central to north-central WI as skies clear and
winds diminish late tonight into early Wednesday morning.

Gusty Winds Wednesday...
Behind the cold front on Wednesday, clearing skies in the morning
will promote strong daytime surface heating and efficient 
boundary- layer mixing. Steep low-level lapse rates will support 
gusty west winds of 25 to 30 mph across the area, with localized 
gusts reaching up to 35 knots across north-central Wisconsin where
deeper mixing is anticipated. Highs on Wednesday will warm into 
the mid 70s to low 80s. Winds will diminish Wednesday night as 
high pressure slides into the region, bringing clear skies and 
cooler overnight lows in the mid 40s to mid 50s.

Thunderstorm Potential Friday through Monday...
Moving into the late-week period, the upper-level flow pattern from 
Thursday through Monday will feature general troughing spanning from 
the Pacific Northwest to eastern Canada, juxtaposed against a 
suppressed subtropical ridge over the southern tier of the country. 
A shortwave lifting northeast across the northern Plains into south-
central Canada will propel a cold front through the forecast area 
late Friday night into Saturday morning. While synoptic dynamics are 
respectable, a narrow moisture axis with precipitable water values 
around 140 percent of normal will precede the boundary. Thunderstorm 
potential will be constrained by a significant cap centered near 800 
mb, with elevated CAPE of 600 to 800 J/kg located above the 
inversion. Instability is expected to diminish rapidly with eastward 
extent into Saturday morning, keeping the severe weather threat low.

For the remainder of the extended period Sunday into Monday, the 
cold front is forecast to stall and return northward as a warm 
front as a wave of surface low pressure tracks northeast along the
boundary across the region. Considerable model spread remains 
regarding the exact track and timing of the surface low, resulting
in low confidence in specific timing details. However, robust 
synoptic forcing and modest MU CAPE generate a notable heavy rain 
signal in the Extreme Forecast Index (EFI) across northern and 
northwest Wisconsin. Elevated convection capable of producing 
heavy rainfall will need to be monitored over the coming days. 
High temperatures will generally average in the upper 60s to mid 
70s through the weekend and early next week.
